newsitem.title: USA: Bankrupt Marvel battles with bondholders.
newsitem.headline: Bankrupt Marvel battles with bondholders.

text.p: Marvel Entertainment Group Inc, once a stock market superhero, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy on Friday, as waning interest in sports trading cards and unsuccessful acquisitions forced the company to seek fresh capital.
The filing would allow Marvel to carry out -- upon the bankruptcy court's approval -- a $525 million recapitalization plan, which would dilute the ownership of public stockholders.
It also promises to keep tensions high between Ron Perelman, who controls a majority stake in Marvel, and Marvel bondholders, including financier Carl Icahn.

Marvel Entertainment, which publishes comic books such as Spider Man and the X-Men, and its three holding companies filed for reorganization under Chapter 11 of the U.S. Bankruptcy Code. In a statement, Marvel said it was forced to file because holders of bonds issued by its holding companies failed to reach agreement on alternatives to its reorganization plan.
More than a month ago, owners of Marvel holding company bonds were asked to support Marvel's plan by waiving certain restrictions contained in the bonds.

But bondholders balked at the proposal, made by Perelman, to buy newly issued shares of Marvel at a steep discount to the market price. That move would massively dilute the value of Marvel's current stock, which backs the company's bonds.

"The failure to reach agreement with bondholders, many of whom are so-called 'vulture investors' who recently accumulated the bonds, delayed Marvel from moving forward with its plan in a timely fashion," Marvel said in its statement.

Icahn responded with a statement saying it was "reprehensible" that Marvel filed for bankruptcy and that the company "completely ignored a far more equitable alternative that had been presented and remains available." He was not immediately available to provide details of that plan.

"It is patently clear that Ron Perelman has adopted this course to realize a windfall profit for himself at the expense of those to whom he owes a fiduciary responsibility," said Icahn, who holds an undisclosed amount of Marvel bonds through his High River Ltd Partnership.
A spokesperson for Perelman did not return calls seeking comment.

Several shareholder suits also have been filed seeking to block Marvel from selling newly issued shares to Perelman at discount prices. The shareholders contended that the public stake would fall to 4 percent from 20 percent, while Perelman's 80 percent stake in Marvel would remain protected.

"We would have preferred to recapitalize Marvel without having to seek the aid of the court, but the actions and positions taken by the bondholders prevented that approach," Marvel Chairman Scott Sassa said.

Marvel and other trading card companies, such as Topps Co Inc, have suffered amid a slump in the sports memorabilia market. Marvel has also struggled under an onerous debt structure and tripped on acquisitions that failed to meet expectations, analysts said.

"When you have such a large confluence of factors, you can't create earnings if the top line isn't reaching what it is supposed to," David Leibowitz of Burham Securities said. "The situation went from bad to worse. It's not an overnight occurence," he said.

On Friday, Marvel's stock was not available for trading on the New York Stock Exchange. The shares closed Thursday at 2-3/8, a little higher than their 52-week low of 2-1/4 but far below the 52-week high of 13-3/8.
Under the proposed financial restructuring plan, Perelman's Andrews Group Inc will invest $365 million in new equity in Marvel in exchange for newly issued shares of Marvel common stock.

As part of the deal, Andrews also will merge Marvel's operations with Toy Biz Inc. Andrews on Friday finalized an agreement to acquire all class A shares of Toy Biz held by public shareholders for $22.50 each.
Marvel could use the Toy Biz's cash flow to shore up its weak finances, analysts said.
Marvel will continue to operate during the bankruptcy proceeding, with the help of $100 million in debtor-in-possession financing. The DIP financing remains subject to court approval.
Marvel's lender group also has agreed to provide $160 million in fresh financing for Marvel's new strategic investment program and working capital requirements.
